problem: Existing object-goal navigation planners, whether training-free (StructNav), RL-based or zero-shot, pick subgoals with local, myopic heuristics such as nearest frontier or greedy detours to semantically related landmarks. They ignore the global visiting order of observed landmarks and how a finite travel budget should be split between exploring new areas and exploiting known landmarks. This breaks down in large workspaces of hundreds of meters or thousands of m².
motivation: With long-range landmark sensing, many landmarks become known at once. Sources include aerial drone views, prior maps and wide-angle views taken before entering a room. When the landmark range L is much larger than the target-detection range R, the landmark visiting order optimization problem (LOOP) dominates efficiency, and its complexity grows with the map horizon. The authors argue that orienteering and multi-objective optimization solvers from operations research are largely unused in ON and could replace myopic behavior with globally coherent plans.
key_idea: Reformulate single-target ObjectNav as a multi-objective problem (explore frontiers vs. exploit observed landmarks) and solve the exploitation part as a variable-horizon, budget-constrained Set Orienteering Problem. The graph's viewpoint clusters surround observed landmarks, a VNS-SOP metaheuristic solves it, and the plan is re-solved as the incremental landmark map grows.
insight: Set-orienteering semantics (visiting any one viewpoint of a landmark cluster collects its reward) plus explicit budget-aware global ordering capture the structure of landmark-guided search that greedy frontier selection misses. In the main 2D experiments MOON beats a frontier planner by roughly 0.18–0.23 SPL in all six (R, M) settings. Its SPL also rises with more landmarks at R=3 (0.8315→0.8734 for M=10→20), while the frontier planner stays near 0.61–0.65. Coverage-style sweeper and TSP planners proved unsuitable because they produce overly dense floor-sweeping paths. Appendix B suggests the solver's non-myopic decisions can be amortized into a cost-biased transformer: 1.137 vs 1.482 'SPL' for the expert, at 0.034 s vs 0.384 s latency. Appendix A claims budget-aware switching beats fixed-rule switching (explore-then-exploit, or detour-on-detection), and that repeated bidirectional switching is close but costlier; these claims come without numbers.
method: Incremental landmark map (VHIM/QOM): starts as a blank object grid map; landmarks and walls detected within the long-range radius L are added incrementally, and repeated observations are ignored (zero gain). In the conceptual prototype, QOM scores each semantic point-cloud cluster's relevance to the target via BERT embeddings and cosine similarity (following StructNav/ALCON).

Navigation graph construction: nodes are viewpoints within radius R of observed landmarks, grouped into clusters by landmark ID that share one utility score; edges carry Dijkstra (or A*) path costs, computed with one Dijkstra run per node.

Variable-horizon SOP: an ILP maximizes Σ p_i y_i under start/end, degree-consistency, travel-budget B and MTZ subtour-elimination constraints over observed nodes V'. It is solved with the VNS-SOP solver of Pěnička et al. 2019 and re-solved as the map grows. Appendix A uses a scalarized objective J = w_cost·Cost − w_reward·Reward with w_cost=0.2, w_reward=0.8.

Budget-aware mode switching (Appendix A): for each exploitation fraction p ∈ {0,0.2,…,1}, V(p) = η_explore·(1−p)B + R_ext(pB), where R_ext is obtained by running the SOP planner with budget pB. The agent picks the argmax and switches between an exploration mode and a target-seeking (SOP) mode, with hysteresis to prevent chattering.

Learned helper modules (Appendix A): CPC is a 3-conv-layer CNN on 50×50 map crops that predicts frontier coverage gain, supervised by ray-casting, and filters low-yield frontiers. DCTP scores the traversability of unknown cells along the all-free shortest path and accepts the path if the product of probabilities exceeds 0.5. NBVP samples candidate viewpoints from a learned P(x_target | landmark) and adds them as SOP nodes. Training uses Adam, MSE, lr 1e-3, batch 64.

Neural-SOP distillation (Appendix B): a 6-layer, 8-head, d_model=128 transformer takes node features [x, y, normalized reward]. Attention is biased by M_ij = log(normalized cost + ε). It is trained with cross-entropy to imitate the next node chosen by vns-sop, and a budget-feasibility logit mask (c_cur,j + c_j,goal ≤ B_rem) guarantees feasible completion.

setting.backbone: VNS-SOP metaheuristic solver (Pěnička et al. 2019), non-learned, in the main method. The appendix variants add small CNNs (CPC/DCTP/NBVP) and a distilled 6-layer cost-biased transformer (Neural-SOP). The conceptual front-end is StructNav (Mask R-CNN, RTAB-Map, BERT) but is not used in the reported experiments.
setting.model_size: n/a (solver); distilled student: 6-layer, 8-head, d_model=128 transformer (parameter count not given)
setting.training_data: None for the main MOON planner (training-free). Appendix A: CPC/DCTP trained offline on simulated ray-casting labels; the exploration-efficiency predictor is learned from simulated data. Appendix B: SOP instances generated from 10 binary maps (15 clusters, ≤5 nodes each, budgets in [500,5000]) and labeled by vns-sop. The text says 'up to 1,000 instances' and also '10,000 samples', with 8,000 for training and 2,000 for validation.
setting.observation: Main text: abstract 2D world with circular sensing, i.e. a long-range landmark detector (L=100/200 m) and a short-range target detector (R=3 m, results also given for R=10), plus known pose. Appendix A: 360° depth up to 8 m for mapping, 90°-FOV landmark detection at 8 m, and a 90° target cone at 1 m (forward RGB-like sensor + omnidirectional depth). Appendix B: range sensing + depth fused into a semantic occupancy grid.
setting.action_space: High-level subgoal selection: the next viewpoint node on the landmark navigation graph or a frontier cell, executed by a Dijkstra/A* global planner and a local planner.
setting.simulator: Custom 2D synthetic 300 m × 300 m multi-room grid world (main text). Appendix A: procedurally generated ProcTHOR-extended scenes (~56.8 m × 56.8 m, ~50 rooms). Appendix B: an unnamed 'photorealistic indoor simulator' with large layouts (~2,384 m²).
setting.privileged: Robot self-location assumed known. Landmark and target detection are idealized, noise-free fixed-radius sensors in the main 2D experiments. A given target–landmark co-occurrence prior P(Target|Landmark) is used in Appendix A.

numbers_note: The paper has no results tables. The main-text numbers come from a bullet list with SPL printed as fractions (e.g. 0.8315) and are converted to 0-100 here. The hyperparameters list L=100,200 m and R=3 m, yet no L=200 results are reported and three settings use R=10. Appendix A's ProcTHOR-based multi-target SPL_multi study (9 target types × 10 environments, 1,200 m budget) gives no numbers: it claims the highest average SPL_multi, 'more than doubles' the strongest baseline in many classes, and <4 s per subgoal; its ablations and ultra-large-scale results are only described qualitatively or said to be in plots. Appendix B prints SPL values above 1 (1.482 / 1.137 / 0.261), which is inconsistent with standard SPL, so they are recorded as SPL_raw. SR and Reward Ratio are defined but not reported. Latency claims are internally inconsistent (8 ms vs 0.034 s; 'several seconds' vs 0.384 s), and the '≥80% of expert quality' claim conflicts with 1.137/1.482 ≈ 76.7%.
results: In the 300 m × 300 m synthetic 2D world, MOON reaches SPL 0.8188–0.8734 versus 0.6083–0.6540 for frontier-based exploration across all six (L, R, M) settings; for example, at L=100, R=3, M=20 it scores 0.8734 vs 0.6473. Sweeper and TSP coverage planners were judged unusable because they produce overly dense paths. In Appendix B, the distilled Neural-SOP reaches 'SPL' 1.137 vs 1.482 for the VNS expert and 0.261 for nearest frontier, cutting planning latency from 0.384 s to 0.034 s. Appendix A claims budget-aware switching yields the best SPL_multi on large ProcTHOR-style scenes but reports no numbers.
limitations: Evaluation is highly idealized and non-standard: an abstract 2D world with circular noise-free sensors, point landmarks and known pose. MOON is compared only against a frontier planner. There are no standard ObjectNav benchmarks (HM3D/MP3D) and no comparison to StructNav or other modern ON methods, even though the prototype is described as built on StructNav.

Reporting is inconsistent and incomplete: settings don't match the stated hyperparameters, Appendix A has no quantitative results, Appendix B's SPL exceeds 1, latency and data-count figures conflict, and the appendices read as separate works with different setups and metrics.
No real-robot results (only 'preliminary real-world trials' mentioned). Performance variance grows in ultra-large environments, and hyperparameters tuned at one scale do not transfer.
